intro: Historians of fighting arts rarely watch the past directly. They work from what survives: a painted manuscript in Leeds, a Ming general's handbook, a swordsman's scrolls from Kumamoto, a boxing belt from London, a cup given by a Japanese crown prince, and early films shot in New Jersey and Nevada. Each object was made for its own reasons, and each leaves gaps.

Fighting arts also have a history of refusals. A champion refused Black challengers in the 1880s. Congress refused to let fight films cross state lines in 1912. Muhammad Ali refused the draft in 1967, and the Supreme Court sided with him in 1971. Iceland, Sweden and Norway each closed the ring by law, then later reopened it under licenses.

In this unit you will read objects and legal records as evidence. You will be able to date a source, say what it proves and what it cannot, and explain who held power over a sport at a given moment. You will also compare how the United States, Iceland, Sweden and Norway wrote laws about the ring.
bigQuestion: How do surviving objects and recorded refusals show who shaped the history of fighting arts?

write.prompt: Argue from the unit's records: which kind of evidence tells us more about who controlled a fighting art, an object (a manuscript, belt, cup or film) or a legal record (a statute, conviction, court ruling or ban)? Cite two or three by name and date.
tips: Name each source with its date, such as the Sims Act of 1912 or MS I.33 of about 1300.
Say what each source proves and what it leaves out.
Name who held power in each case: a champion, a patron, a court or a parliament.
Label legends as legends and set them beside dated records.

title: Object and Plan

chapters.title: Objects That Keep a Record
chapters.bigQuestion: What can a book, a prize or a strip of film prove about the history of a fighting art, and what can it not prove?

story.title: A Manuscript Under Glass
story.kicker: A handwritten book about sword and buckler has survived for about seven hundred years.
paragraphs: In the Royal Armouries museum in Leeds, England, curators keep a small Latin manuscript catalogued as MS I.33. Scholars date it to around 1300. Its painted pages show a priest teaching a student to fight with a sword and a small round shield called a buckler.

Nobody knows for certain who made the book or where it was first used. Historians think it came from a German-speaking land. It passed through several owners over the centuries before it reached a British museum collection.

The manuscript is an object, and objects survive for reasons of their own. A rich owner paid for fine paint. A library kept it dry. Thousands of plainer notebooks, and most teaching that was never written down, did not survive at all.

Historians of martial arts work with objects like this one: books, belts, cups, masks, photographs and films. Each one can answer some questions well. Each one also leaves gaps, and a careful reader names those gaps before drawing a conclusion.
story.think: If only rich owners could pay for painted books, whose fighting arts are most likely missing from the record of 1300?

lessons.title: The Leeds Sword Book
lessons.mainIdea: Royal Armouries MS I.33, from around 1300, is the oldest surviving European book about fighting with weapons.
reading: A *fencing manual* is a book that records a system of armed combat. In German such a book is called a *Fechtbuch*, meaning fight book. The oldest known European example is Royal Armouries MS I.33, dated by scholars to around 1300 and held today in Leeds, England.

The manuscript mixes Latin text with painted figures. Most pages show a priest, called sacerdos in the text, and a student, called scholaris. Near the end, a woman named Walpurgis appears in the pictures, which makes the book an early record of a woman shown in armed practice.

The book survives as a single copy. Historians cannot name its author, and its exact place of origin is still debated, though most point to a German-speaking region. That is typical of an *artifact*: it proves that someone recorded this teaching, but it does not show how widely it was taught.

words.d: a book that records a system of armed combat, often with pictures
German for fight book; the name for late medieval and Renaissance combat manuals
an object made by people that historians study as evidence

look.title: One Copy, Many Questions
look.text: A museum holds one painted book from around 1300. It shows a priest and a student with sword and buckler. No second copy is known. No author's name is written in it. Its first owner is unknown.
look.prompt: List two questions this book can answer well and two questions it cannot answer at all.

check.q: What makes Royal Armouries MS I.33 important?
choices: It is the oldest surviving European fencing manual
It is the first judo rule book
It is a Chinese military treatise
It records the first Olympic fencing event
check.why: MS I.33, from around 1300, is the oldest known European book on armed combat.

check.q: Who are the main figures painted in MS I.33?
check.why: The pages mostly show a priest (sacerdos) and a student (scholaris).

check.q: What does the word Fechtbuch mean?
check.why: Fechtbuch is German for fight book.

lessons.title: Fiore's Flower of Battle
lessons.mainIdea: Fiore dei Liberi, an Italian master, wrote the Fior di Battaglia around 1400, and several copies survive in museums and libraries.
reading: Fiore dei Liberi was a fencing master from Friuli, in northeastern Italy. Around 1400 he produced a manuscript called *Fior di Battaglia*, the Flower of Battle. One copy is dedicated to Niccolò III d'Este, the lord of Ferrara, which ties the work to a court patron.

Unlike MS I.33, Fiore's work survives in more than one copy. One is held by the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles and another by the Morgan Library and Museum in New York. The copies differ in their pictures and text, so scholars compare them line by line.

In his introduction Fiore described learning from many masters and said he had fought several duels. Historians treat such claims as the author's own account. A *patron*, a wealthy person who paid for a book, often shaped how an author presented himself on its pages.

words.d: Italian for Flower of Battle; Fiore dei Liberi's combat manuscript from around 1400
a wealthy person who paid for an artist's or writer's work
a book written and copied by hand

look.title: Two Copies Side by Side
look.text: Copy A, in Los Angeles, has one set of pictures and short verses. Copy B, in New York, arranges some of the same material differently and adds or drops some figures. Both carry Fiore's name.
look.prompt: Why might a historian want to see both copies before saying what Fiore taught?

check.q: Where did Fiore dei Liberi come from?
check.why: Fiore was a master from Friuli in northeastern Italy.

check.q: Why do scholars compare copies of the Fior di Battaglia?
choices: The copies differ in pictures and text
It was printed on a machine
check.why: Several hand-made copies survive, and they are not identical.

check.q: What is a patron?
choices: a student in a sword school
a wealthy person who paid for a work
check.why: A patron paid for a book or artwork, like the lord of Ferrara for Fiore.

lessons.title: A Ming General's Handbook
lessons.mainIdea: Qi Jiguang's military handbook of the 1560s includes a chapter on boxing, one of the oldest dated Chinese texts on unarmed practice.
reading: Qi Jiguang (1528–1588) was a general of China's Ming dynasty. In the 1550s and 1560s he fought raiders along China's southeast coast, whom Ming records called *wokou*. Around 1560 he wrote the *Jixiao Xinshu*, often translated as New Book of Effective Discipline.

Most of the book is about training soldiers, organizing units and using weapons. One chapter is about boxing. Qi wrote that boxing did not seem useful for battle, but that it trained the body and built confidence for beginners. The book also covers spears, swords, halberds and the organization of troops.

The chapter names several boxing families known in Qi's day and pictures a set of postures. Historians value it because it has a firm date and a named author. Many later schools told origin legends, but Qi's book shows what one army officer actually wrote down in the 1560s.

words.d: a Ming military handbook written by general Qi Jiguang around 1560
the Ming name for coastal raiders who attacked China's southeast in the 1500s
the ruling house of China from 1368 to 1644

look.title: A General Judges Boxing
look.text: Boxing seems to have little use in great battles. Still, it exercises the hands and feet and trains the body, so it is a good way for beginners to start learning skill.
look.cite: Qi Jiguang, Jixiao Xinshu, chapter on boxing, c. 1560
look.prompt: Why did Qi keep a boxing chapter in a book for soldiers, even though he doubted its use in battle?

check.q: Who wrote the Jixiao Xinshu?
check.why: The Ming general Qi Jiguang wrote it around 1560.

check.q: What did Qi say about boxing?
choices: It trained the body even if it had little use in battle
It came from the Shaolin Monastery
check.why: Qi doubted boxing's use in battle but valued it as training for beginners.

check.q: Why do historians value Qi's boxing chapter?
choices: It has a firm date and a named author
It is the only Ming book
check.why: A dated text by a named author is stronger evidence than a later legend.

lessons.title: Musashi's Book of Five Rings
lessons.mainIdea: Miyamoto Musashi finished the Go Rin no Sho near Kumamoto in 1645, shortly before he died.
reading: Miyamoto Musashi was a Japanese swordsman of the early Edo period. Late in life he lived in Kumamoto, on the island of Kyushu. In the 1640s he wrote *Go Rin no Sho*, the Book of Five Rings, in a cave called Reigandō, according to long tradition. He was born around 1584.

The book has five scrolls, named for Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and the Void. Musashi gave it to his student Terao Magonojō shortly before his death in 1645. The original manuscript does not survive, so modern editions rely on later handwritten copies.

Musashi's own life is known partly from records and partly from later stories, plays and novels. His famous 1612 duel with Sasaki Kojirō is told mainly in sources written long afterward. Historians separate the *scroll* he wrote from the *legend* that grew around him.

words.d: the Book of Five Rings, written by Miyamoto Musashi in the 1640s
a long roll of paper or silk used for writing in East Asia
a story passed down about the past that cannot be fully proven
the era of Tokugawa rule in Japan, 1603 to 1868

look.title: When Four Books Were Written
look.cite: Royal Armouries; J. Paul Getty Museum; standard histories of Qi Jiguang and Miyamoto Musashi
look.prompt: How many years separate the oldest and the newest book on this chart?

check.q: When did Musashi finish the Book of Five Rings?
check.why: Musashi gave the finished book to his student shortly before he died in 1645.

check.q: Why do modern editions of Go Rin no Sho rely on copies?
check.why: The original manuscript is lost, so editors use later handwritten copies.

check.q: What do the five scrolls of the book take their names from?
choices: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and the Void
check.why: The scrolls are named Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and the Void.

lessons.title: The Lonsdale Belt
lessons.mainIdea: Britain's National Sporting Club created the Lonsdale Belt in 1909, and a boxer could keep it by winning three title fights in one weight class.
reading: The National Sporting Club was a private boxing club in Covent Garden, London. In 1909 it began awarding a belt for British champions. The belt was named for Hugh Lowther, the fifth Earl of Lonsdale, who supported the club. The first winner was the lightweight Freddie Welsh, in 1909.

The belt came with a rule. A *champion* who won three title fights in the same weight class could keep the belt for good. That rule rewarded boxers who defended a title, not just those who won it once. Welsh was a Welsh boxer whose real name was Frederick Hall Thomas.

The British Boxing Board of Control, formed in 1929, later took over the belt and still awards it. Many Lonsdale Belts now sit in family homes and museum cases. Each belt is a *trophy*, and like a certificate it records a *sanctioning body*, a date and a weight.

words.d: a British boxing championship belt first awarded by the National Sporting Club in 1909
the winner of a title in a sport or weight class
a cup, belt or other object given as a prize
an organization that approves contests and recognizes titles

look.title: Reading a Belt
look.text: A boxing belt in a case carries a name, a weight class and several engraved dates. A label says the boxer won three title fights and kept the belt. The belt's maker and the club that gave it are named on the back.
look.prompt: What facts could a historian check in other records using only what is written on this belt?

check.q: Who first awarded the Lonsdale Belt?
choices: the British Boxing Board of Control
check.why: The National Sporting Club in London first awarded it in 1909.

check.q: How could a boxer keep a Lonsdale Belt for good?
choices: by winning three title fights in one weight class
check.why: Three title wins in the same weight class let a champion keep the belt.

check.q: Who was the first Lonsdale Belt winner?
check.why: Lightweight Freddie Welsh won the first belt in 1909.

lessons.title: A Cup for Sumo's Top Division
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1909 sumo has named a champion of each tournament, and a cup from the imperial family has been given to the top-division winner since the 1920s.
reading: Sumo in Tokyo moved into a new indoor hall, the Kokugikan in Ryōgoku, in 1909. That year the sport began to recognize one wrestler as the winner of each tournament. The Japanese word for this championship is *yūshō*. Before 1909, sumo records listed each wrestler's wins and losses, but no single tournament winner was named.

In 1925 Crown Prince Hirohito, who later became emperor, watched sumo and gave money for a prize. The trophy made from that gift became known as the *Emperor's Cup*. It is presented to the winner of the top division, called *makuuchi*, at the end of each grand tournament.

The cup is large and heavy, and winners hold it up for photographs on the last day. It links professional sumo, run today by the Japan Sumo Association, to the imperial family. The object shows how a sport gained status by attaching a national symbol to its prize.

words.d: the championship of a sumo tournament, won by the wrestler with the best record
the trophy given to the top-division sumo champion, begun with a gift from Crown Prince Hirohito in 1925
the top division of professional sumo

look.title: A Gift and a Status
look.text: In 1925 a crown prince watches sumo and gives money. A cup is made. Decades later, every top-division champion lifts that cup in front of cameras at the end of a tournament.
look.prompt: How might a prize from the imperial family change how the public sees a professional sport?

check.q: What is a yūshō?
choices: the championship of a sumo tournament
check.why: Yūshō is the tournament championship, recognized since 1909.

check.q: Whose gift began the Emperor's Cup?
check.why: Crown Prince Hirohito gave money for a prize in 1925.

check.q: What is makuuchi?
choices: the top division of professional sumo
check.why: Makuuchi is the top division, whose winner receives the Emperor's Cup.

lessons.title: The Fencing Mask
lessons.mainIdea: Wire-mesh fencing masks spread in France in the late 1700s, and they made faster practice with blunted weapons much safer.
reading: For centuries, fencers practiced with blunted swords and little face protection. Teachers limited attacks to the body because an eye injury could be fatal. That limit shaped how people practiced and how contests were judged. Fencing had long been taught in European cities by licensed masters and guilds.

In the late 1700s, French fencing teachers began using masks of woven wire mesh. Many histories credit the Paris master Texier de La Boëssière with making the *mask* popular. The mesh let a fencer see and breathe while it stopped a blade from reaching the face.

Masks changed the practice room. With the face protected, fencers could exchange attacks more freely, and the rules of *foil* fencing developed around that faster play. The mask is a small object that stands for a large change: safety equipment making a new kind of contest possible.

words.d: in fencing, a helmet of wire mesh that protects the face and head
a light fencing weapon, and the contest fought with it
made dull or capped so that it cannot cut or pierce

look.title: Before and After the Mesh
look.text: Room one, about 1750: fencers wear no face cover, and the teacher stops practice often. Room two, about 1800: fencers wear wire masks, and exchanges run longer before the teacher calls a halt.
look.prompt: What changed between the two rooms, and why did one object make that change possible?

check.q: When did wire-mesh fencing masks spread in France?
check.why: French teachers adopted wire-mesh masks in the late 1700s.

check.q: Who is often credited with making the fencing mask popular?
check.why: Many histories credit the Paris master La Boëssière.

check.q: How did the mask change fencing practice?
choices: It let fencers exchange attacks more freely
It ended the use of foils
It made fencing a team sport
It replaced the strip with a ring
check.why: With the face protected, practice could be faster and freer.

lessons.title: Muybridge Photographs Motion
lessons.mainIdea: Eadweard Muybridge's Animal Locomotion (1887) included sequences of men boxing, wrestling and fencing, among the first photographs to freeze combat sports in motion.
reading: Eadweard Muybridge was an English-born photographer working in the United States. In the 1880s the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia supported his study of movement. He lined up many cameras and triggered them one after another to record a moving body.

In 1887 he published *Animal Locomotion*, a set of 781 plates. The subjects included horses, birds and people doing everyday tasks. Some plates show men boxing, wrestling and fencing, each broken into a row of still frames. Other plates show runners, jumpers and people climbing stairs.

The plates were made for science, not for sport. Still, they are early photographic records of how athletes of the 1880s dressed and where they stood in a room. A *plate* in this sense is one printed page of images, and each one was staged for the camera.

words.d: Eadweard Muybridge's 1887 set of 781 photographic plates showing people and animals in motion
one printed page of pictures in a book or set
arranged on purpose for a camera or audience

look.title: A Staged Record
look.text: A plate from 1887 shows two men wrestling in front of a grid-marked wall. Twelve small frames run left to right. The men were asked to perform for a row of cameras in Philadelphia.
look.prompt: What can this plate tell us about the 1880s, and what might be different from a real contest of the time?

check.q: Which university supported Muybridge's motion studies?
check.why: The University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia supported the work that became Animal Locomotion.

check.q: How many plates were in Animal Locomotion?
check.why: The 1887 set held 781 plates.

check.q: Why must a historian remember the plates were staged?
choices: The men performed for cameras, not in a real contest
check.why: Staged images show posed action, which may differ from a real match.

lessons.title: Edison Films a Boxing Match
lessons.mainIdea: In 1894 Thomas Edison's company filmed a boxing exhibition in its Black Maria studio, with rounds shortened to fit the camera.
reading: Thomas Edison's company built a film studio in West Orange, New Jersey, in 1893. Workers called it the *Black Maria* because it was dark and cramped like a police wagon. Its roof opened, and the building turned to follow the sun. It was among the first buildings made only for shooting films.

In September 1894 heavyweight champion James J. Corbett boxed Peter Courtney in the studio. The film was shown in a *Kinetoscope*, a cabinet with a peephole that one viewer looked into at a time. Each round was shortened so it fit on the film the machine could hold.

The bout was arranged for the camera, and viewers paid to watch each round. That made boxing one of the first subjects sold as moving pictures. Historians see here an early tie between combat sport and film, a tie that later drew the attention of lawmakers.

words.d: Thomas Edison's film studio in West Orange, New Jersey, built in 1893
an early film viewer that one person watched through a peephole
a match held to be watched, often without an official title at stake

look.title: A Fight Built for the Camera
look.text: A champion boxes in a small studio with an open roof. The rounds are cut short so each one fits the film. Later, customers pay a coin for each round they watch in a cabinet.
look.prompt: How did the camera change the shape of the match itself?

check.q: Where was the Black Maria studio?
check.why: Edison's company built the studio in West Orange in 1893.

check.q: Why were the rounds of the 1894 bout shortened?
choices: to fit the film the camera could hold
because of a new state law
check.why: Each round had to fit the Kinetoscope's short length of film.

check.q: What was a Kinetoscope?
choices: a cabinet viewer for one person
check.why: Viewers watched Kinetoscope films one at a time through a peephole.

lessons.title: The Veriscope in Carson City
lessons.mainIdea: The 1897 Corbett–Fitzsimmons fight in Carson City, Nevada, was filmed on wide film and shown as one of the longest films of its time.
reading: In 1897 Nevada passed a law allowing prizefights, when most states banned them. On March 17, 1897, James J. Corbett defended his heavyweight title against Bob Fitzsimmons in Carson City. Fitzsimmons won in the fourteenth round. The fight took place on St. Patrick's Day before a crowd in an outdoor arena.

Promoters filmed the fight with a camera called the *Veriscope*, which used unusually wide film. The finished picture ran well over an hour, making it one of the longest films made up to that time. It was shown in theaters across the country. Enoch J. Rector led the filming.

Fitzsimmons was born in Cornwall, England, and had boxed in New Zealand and Australia before coming to America. It showed that a filmed bout could reach far more people than a crowd in one arena. A *promoter*, the business person who organizes a match, now had two products to sell: the fight and its film.

words.d: the wide-film camera used to record the 1897 Corbett–Fitzsimmons fight
a business person who organizes and sells a match
a boxing match fought for money
the prize money paid to the fighters

look.title: Early Combat on Camera
look.cite: Library of Congress, Edison motion picture collection; University of Pennsylvania Archives
look.prompt: How many years passed between Muybridge's plates and the first full-length fight film?

check.q: Who won the 1897 fight in Carson City?
check.why: Fitzsimmons beat Corbett in the fourteenth round.

check.q: Why could the fight take place in Nevada?
choices: Nevada had passed a law allowing prizefights
It was held on a ship
Nevada was not yet a state
check.why: Nevada legalized prizefighting in 1897.

check.q: What is a promoter?
choices: a business person who organizes and sells a match
check.why: Promoters organize matches and, after 1897, often sold the films too.

review.why: MS I.33 dates to around 1300, far older than the others.

review.q: What do the Fior di Battaglia and the Book of Five Rings have in common?
review.why: Fiore's work survives in several copies; Musashi's original is lost and later copies remain.

review.q: Which writer was a Ming general?
review.why: Qi Jiguang led Ming troops against coastal raiders.

review.q: What do the Lonsdale Belt and the Emperor's Cup both record?
choices: a championship recognized by a governing body or patron
review.why: Both are prizes that record who won a recognized title.

review.q: What did wire-mesh masks make possible in fencing?
choices: longer, freer practice with the face protected
review.why: Protecting the face let fencers practice faster exchanges.

review.q: Put these in order: Edison films Corbett; Muybridge publishes plates; Veriscope films Carson City.
review.why: Muybridge published in 1887, Edison filmed in 1894 and the Veriscope in 1897.

review.q: Why is a legend about Musashi weaker evidence than his own book?
choices: Legends were written long after the events
review.why: Many Musashi stories come from much later plays and novels.

review.q: Which object linked a professional sport to Japan's imperial family?
review.why: The Emperor's Cup began with Crown Prince Hirohito's gift in 1925.

chapters.title: Bans, Color Lines and Refusals
chapters.bigQuestion: When a champion, a court or a nation refused a fight, who gained power over the sport, and who lost it?

story.title: A Film Stopped at the State Line
story.kicker: In 1910 a boxing film became a question for Congress.
paragraphs: On July 4, 1910, Jack Johnson, the first Black world heavyweight champion, fought James J. Jeffries in Reno, Nevada. Jeffries had retired undefeated and came back to fight Johnson. Newspapers had spent months calling him the hope of white America.

Johnson won in the fifteenth round. That night and in the days after, white crowds attacked Black Americans in many cities, and people were killed. Some city governments then banned showing the film of the fight.

Two years later, in 1912, Congress passed the Sims Act. It made it a federal crime to carry films of prizefights across state lines. The law stayed in place until 1940. Its chief sponsor was Representative Thetus W. Sims of Tennessee.

The story shows that a fight can be refused in many ways. A champion can refuse a challenger. A court or a Congress can refuse a film. A person can refuse a government's order. A nation can refuse the ring itself. Each refusal changed who controlled a fighting art.
story.think: Why would lawmakers try to stop a film instead of the fight itself?

sections.title: A Title Crosses the Color Line

lessons.title: Sullivan Refuses a Challenger
lessons.mainIdea: Heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan refused to fight Black challengers, including the respected boxer Peter Jackson.
reading: In the 1880s John L. Sullivan of Boston was the most famous boxer in the United States. As heavyweight champion, he chose whom he would fight. He publicly refused to box any Black challenger, a practice later called the *color line*. He held the title from 1882 to 1892.

Peter Jackson was born in 1861 on St. Croix, then part of the Danish West Indies. He built his career in Australia and was one of the best heavyweights of his time. In 1891 in San Francisco, Jackson fought James J. Corbett for 61 rounds, and the bout was ruled a *no contest*.

Sullivan never fought Jackson. Because a champion controlled his own title, one man's refusal could keep a whole group of boxers from a chance at the top prize. The color line in heavyweight boxing held until 1908, when Jack Johnson finally got his title fight. Jackson died in Australia in 1901.

words.d: a racial barrier that kept Black athletes from competing against white athletes or for certain titles
a ruling that a bout has no winner, often after it is stopped
a fighter who seeks a match against the current champion

look.title: Who Holds the Door
look.text: In the 1880s no commission or federation ruled heavyweight boxing. The champion decided whom to meet. A top Black boxer asks for a title fight. The champion says no, and no body above him can order the match.
look.prompt: How did the lack of a governing body make the color line easier to keep?

check.q: What was the color line in boxing?
choices: a racial barrier that blocked Black challengers
check.why: The color line was a racial barrier that kept Black boxers from title chances.

check.q: Where was Peter Jackson born?
choices: St. Croix, in the Danish West Indies
check.why: Jackson was born on St. Croix in 1861.

check.q: What happened in Jackson's 1891 bout with Corbett?
choices: It lasted 61 rounds and was ruled a no contest
check.why: The San Francisco bout went 61 rounds and ended as a no contest.

lessons.title: Johnson Wins in Sydney
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson became the first Black world heavyweight champion by beating Tommy Burns in Sydney, Australia, in 1908.
reading: Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878. By the early 1900s he was one of the best heavyweights in the world, but champions kept refusing him. He followed champion Tommy Burns, a Canadian, across the world to demand a fight. Burns held the title from 1906 to 1908.

On December 26, 1908, Johnson fought Burns in Sydney, Australia. Police stopped the fight in the fourteenth round, and Johnson was named the winner. He became the first Black world *heavyweight* champion, breaking the color line in boxing's top division.

Many white newspapers reacted with anger. Writers called for a former champion to return and take the title back. That campaign led to the 1910 fight in Reno, and the phrase *Great White Hope* came from it. Former champion James J. Jeffries, then retired on his farm in California, became the man they chose.

words.d: the heaviest weight class in boxing, with no upper weight limit
a phrase from the 1900s for a white boxer promoted to take the title from Jack Johnson
the official recognition of a champion in a weight class

check.why: Johnson beat Canadian champion Tommy Burns in Sydney in 1908.

lessons.title: A Conviction and a Pardon
lessons.mainIdea: Johnson was convicted in 1913 under the Mann Act in a case widely seen as racially motivated, and he was pardoned after his death in 2018.
reading: The *Mann Act* of 1910 made it a federal crime to transport women across state lines for what the law called immoral purposes. In 1913 a federal jury in Chicago convicted Johnson under this law. His relationships with white women were at the center of the case.

Johnson left the country rather than go to prison. He lost his title to Jess Willard in Havana, Cuba, in 1915. He returned in 1920 and served his sentence in the federal prison at Leavenworth, Kansas. He died in a car crash in 1946. He had been sentenced to one year and a day.

For decades, historians and members of Congress argued that the case was driven by racism. On May 24, 2018, President Donald Trump granted Johnson a posthumous *pardon*, meaning a pardon given after death. The pardon did not erase the years Johnson lost.

words.d: a 1910 federal law on transporting women across state lines, used to convict Jack Johnson in 1913
an official act that forgives a crime and removes its penalty
happening after a person's death

look.title: A Record With Two Dates
look.text: A court record from Chicago, 1913: guilty. A presidential document, 2018: pardoned. Between the two dates, Johnson went into exile, lost his title, served a prison sentence and died.
look.prompt: What does a pardon 105 years after a conviction say about how people judged the first decision?

check.q: In which city was Johnson convicted in 1913?
check.why: A federal jury in Chicago convicted him under the Mann Act.

check.q: What does posthumous mean?
check.why: Johnson's 2018 pardon was posthumous because he died in 1946.

check.q: To whom did Johnson lose the title in 1915?
check.why: Jess Willard beat Johnson in Havana in 1915.

lessons.title: Reno, July 4, 1910
lessons.mainIdea: Johnson's 1910 victory over Jeffries in Reno was followed by racist attacks in many U.S. cities.
reading: James J. Jeffries had retired as heavyweight champion in 1905 without losing a fight. Under public pressure, he agreed to return and fight Johnson. The bout was first planned for San Francisco, but California's governor blocked it, so promoter Tex Rickard moved it to Reno, Nevada.

On July 4, 1910, Johnson won in the fifteenth round. News of the result spread by telegraph within minutes. In many cities across the United States, white crowds attacked Black people who celebrated, and people were killed. The fight took place in an outdoor arena built for the day.

The violence showed how a single sporting result could carry the weight of a nation's racial *hierarchy*, a ranking of groups by power. Officials who could not reverse the result turned instead to the film of it. A *telegraph* line had carried the news; the film would carry the pictures.

words.d: a system that ranks groups of people above or below one another
a system that sent messages over wires using coded electrical signals
stopped competing professionally

check.why: Johnson won in the fifteenth round.

check.why: A hierarchy ranks groups of people by power or status.

lessons.title: The Sims Act of 1912
lessons.mainIdea: The Sims Act of 1912 banned carrying prizefight films across state lines, and it stayed law until 1940.
reading: After Reno, many cities banned showing the Johnson–Jeffries film. In 1912 Congress went further. The *Sims Act* made it a federal crime to transport films of prizefights between states or into the country. Its sponsors were Southern members of Congress.

The law did not ban boxing and did not ban filming a fight. It banned moving the film. Promoters found ways around it, such as filming in one state and showing the film only there. The law was enforced unevenly. Breaking the law could bring a fine or a prison term.

Congress repealed the Sims Act in 1940. By then Joe Louis, a Black heavyweight champion from Detroit, had held the title since 1937. Historians read the Sims Act as a clear case of *federal* power used to control what images of a Black champion Americans could see.

words.d: a 1912 federal law that banned carrying prizefight films across state lines; repealed in 1940
belonging to the national government of the United States
to cancel a law

look.title: What the Law Forbade
look.text: It shall be unlawful to bring into the United States, or to carry from one state to another, any film or picture of any prizefight or encounter of pugilists, meant for public exhibition.
look.cite: Sims Act (1912), U.S. Statutes at Large
look.prompt: Which step did the law forbid: fighting, filming or moving the film? Why might Congress choose that step?

choices: all boxing in the United States
carrying prizefight films across state lines
check.why: The 1912 law banned transporting fight films between states or into the country.

check.q: When was the Sims Act repealed?
check.why: Congress repealed the Sims Act in 1940.

check.q: Who held the heavyweight title when the Sims Act ended?
check.why: Joe Louis had been champion since 1937.

lessons.title: Houston, April 1967
lessons.mainIdea: Muhammad Ali refused induction into the U.S. Army in 1967, citing his Muslim faith, and lost his title and his license to box.
reading: Cassius Clay of Louisville, Kentucky, won the Olympic light heavyweight gold medal in Rome in 1960. In 1964 he won the world heavyweight title from Sonny Liston. Soon after, he announced he had joined the Nation of Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali.

During the Vietnam War, the government used the *draft* to call young men into the military. Ali asked to be classified as a *conscientious objector*, a person who refuses military service for reasons of religion or conscience. His request was denied. On April 28, 1967, in Houston, he refused to step forward for induction.

Boxing officials acted within days. The New York State Athletic Commission suspended his license, and the World Boxing Association took away his title. In June 1967 a federal jury convicted him, and he was sentenced to five years in prison, though he stayed free while he appealed.

words.d: a government system that requires people to join the military
a person who refuses military service for reasons of religion or conscience
the formal act of entering military service
to ask a higher court to review a decision

lessons.title: Clay v. United States, 1971
lessons.mainIdea: In 1971 the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Ali's conviction in Clay v. United States, after he had lost more than three years of his career.
reading: Ali did not box from March 1967 to October 1970, when he fought Jerry Quarry in Atlanta. Georgia had no state boxing commission, so a city license made the bout possible. A New York court later ordered the state to restore his license. Quarry was a leading heavyweight from California.

On June 28, 1971, the *Supreme Court* ruled in *Clay v. United States*. The justices voted 8–0 to overturn his conviction, with Justice Thurgood Marshall not taking part. The Court found that the government had not properly explained why it denied his claim as a conscientious objector.

Ali lost his first fight after the ban, to Joe Frazier in 1971. He won the heavyweight title back in 1974 against George Foreman in Kinshasa, Zaire. His case is studied as a refusal that cost an athlete his livelihood and was later upheld by the nation's highest court.

words.d: the highest court in the United States
the 1971 Supreme Court case that overturned Muhammad Ali's draft conviction
to cancel a lower court's decision

check.q: Where did Ali regain the heavyweight title in 1974?
check.why: Ali beat George Foreman in Kinshasa in 1974.

lessons.title: Iceland Bans Boxing, 1956
lessons.mainIdea: Iceland's parliament banned boxing in 1956, and amateur boxing was allowed again only in 2002.
reading: In 1956 the Althing, Iceland's parliament, passed a law banning boxing. The law covered public matches and the teaching of the sport. Supporters of the ban pointed to serious injuries in the ring. The country had become a fully independent republic only twelve years earlier, in 1944, after centuries under Danish rule.

The ban lasted more than four decades. In 2002 the Althing voted to allow *amateur* boxing again. Professional boxing stayed banned in Iceland, so Icelanders who wanted to box for pay had to compete in other countries. That was 46 years after the ban began.

Iceland's ban shows a nation refusing a sport through ordinary *legislation*, a law passed by a parliament. It differs from the Sims Act, which blocked only films, and from a champion's color line, which a single man enforced. It also differs from Ali's case, where a government punished one boxer rather than the sport.

words.d: the parliament of Iceland
competing without being paid
laws made by a parliament or congress

lessons.title: Sweden and Norway Say No to Pros
lessons.mainIdea: Sweden banned professional boxing in 1970 and Norway in 1981, while both kept amateur boxing legal.
reading: Sweden had a famous professional champion, Ingemar Johansson, who won the world heavyweight title from Floyd Patterson in 1959. About a decade later, in 1970, Sweden banned *professional* boxing. Amateur boxing, with its shorter bouts, remained legal.

Norway passed its own ban on professional boxing in 1981. Norwegian boxers who wanted to turn professional had to compete abroad. Supporters of both bans cited medical concerns about repeated blows to the head. Norway's law also covered other sports in which knockouts were the goal.

Both countries later changed course. Sweden allowed professional boxing again in 2006, under a licensing system. Norway's parliament allowed professional matches under new rules in 2016. In both cases a state *license* replaced an outright ban. Sweden's new law took effect in 2007.

words.d: competing for pay as a job
official permission from a government to do something under set rules
an official rule that forbids something

lessons.title: From Ban to License
lessons.mainIdea: Across these cases, refusals often ended not in freedom without rules but in a license, a commission or a court ruling that set new limits.
reading: The color line in the heavyweight division fell in 1908 when a Black challenger finally forced a title fight. The Sims Act of 1912 ended by repeal in 1940. Ali's conviction ended by a Supreme Court ruling in 1971. A different body ended each one: a challenger in the ring, Congress and the Supreme Court.

Nordic bans ended differently. Iceland in 2002, Sweden in 2006 and Norway in 2016 each replaced a ban with rules and *oversight*, meaning ongoing supervision by an official body. Headgear rules, medical checks and licenses took the place of an outright no.

Historians compare such cases to ask who held power at each moment: a champion, a Congress, a commission, a court or a parliament. The answer changed over time. A *regulation*, a rule enforced by an official body, was often the compromise. In the 1880s no official body ruled the heavyweight title, but by the 1960s commissions, associations and courts all claimed a say.

words.d: ongoing supervision by an official body
a rule made and enforced by an official body
a government board that licenses and supervises a sport
